about: Case file CF7 (cf7-cost-of-waiting). Delay economics only; data centers appear only as loads. 'timeline' gives two public context events (DOE, with their primary sources), then the study's steps. Research text: the text of the study step, 'boundary' (its lists) and the study fact's 'what' are approved excerpt sentences (E7, with their revisions after review), word for word; _tests/learn/test_cf7-cost-of-waiting.js checks them. The paper is cited without its title, DOI pending (E7.14). 'idea' is an illustrative toy with invented round numbers (not the study's inputs, equations or results): one large load waits for its grid connection, and the wait is priced in three separate accounts in present value.

timeline.title: The question in time
timeline.lede: Two public events, then the study and its code.

events.label: Data-center electricity use estimated
events.text: DOE releases a Berkeley Lab report: U.S. data centers used about 176 TWh in 2023, about 4.4% of U.S. electricity.

events.label: Federal rulemaking requested
events.text: The Secretary of Energy asks FERC to start a rulemaking on connecting large loads to the interstate transmission system.

source.label: Letter of the Secretary of Energy to FERC, 23 October 2025 (PDF)

events.label: Paper presented
events.text: The delay is priced in three separate accounts: the developer, electricity ratepayers and society.

source.label: Li et al. (2026), North American Power Symposium (NAPS 2026), accepted; DOI pending

boundary.title: Where the result holds
holds: the delay is taken as given, not explained;
the parameters are illustrative, so the study reports which inputs move the result, not a forecast;
the three accounts stay separate, and a net-benefit test says when they may be added.
leaves: why service is late: the interconnection process itself;
whether the network can carry the load (network feasibility);
social costs beyond a single bridge-power example.

idea.title: One large load waits for the grid
idea.note: Illustrative round numbers, not the study's inputs, equations or results.
assumptions: 100 MW, such as a data center or a factory
$45,000 per MW a month (revenue minus operating costs)
$500M of buildings and equipment, carried at the discount rate
$60M; while it waits, the utility's money in them still costs interest
0.5% more each month of waiting, at most 50%; then the upgrades are stranded
decides what share of those utility costs the waiting load pays; other customers pay the rest
on-site generators run half the load during the wait, at $30 per MWh above grid power
0.1 t per MWh more than grid power, had the load been connected on time; $100 per tonne

facts.what: In the study's illustrative base case, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion in present value.
Share of U.S. electricity used by data centers in 2023 (about 176 TWh).
